$comment: What you would actually need to build one. NOT a recipe: recipes are the game's two-input grammar and say how a thing is derived. A needs list is the unbounded, honest answer to 'what goes into one', and exists to drive authoring — the corpus checks itself against it and the gaps fall out. Entries may use a|b alternation where two words mean the same thing. See tools/needs.mjs. Where a component name is ambiguous or is a tag rather than an element (`body` means a car body and a human body; `medicine` is a family, not a thing), the list names what the corpus actually calls it.

abrams_tank.note: A gas turbine borrowed from helicopters — 1,500 horsepower drinking jet fuel.

ac_induction_motor.note: No brushes and no magnets — the rotor is dragged round by a field that is already turning.

accordion.note: Bellows moving air past reeds, and both hands doing different things.

acheulean_handaxe.note: Symmetry struck into stone — the same design for 1.5 million years.

acid_fast_stain.note: A stain that survives an acid wash, which is how tuberculosis is found.

acrylic_fibre.note: Made to be wool, and warm for the same reason.

adder.note: Adding two numbers with nothing but gates.

adobe.note: Earth with enough clay to bind and enough straw to stop it cracking.

advertisement.note: Paying to be in front of somebody who was looking at something else.

agarwood_tree.note: The resin is a wound response, so an uninfected tree is worth almost nothing.

air_brake.note: Westinghouse's 1869 fail-safe: air pressure holds the brakes OFF, so a broken hose stops the train.

air_filter.note: Catching what would otherwise go through at the speed of the intake.

airframe.note: The structure, with the engines and everything else taken off.

ak47.note: A steel-bodied rifle that bleeds propellant gas to cycle its own bolt.

allis_forceps.note: Inward-curving serrated teeth grip fascia without crushing.

altar.note: A raised surface where the thing that matters happens.

alternator.note: The rotor spins electromagnets past fixed windings, avoiding the brushes that wear out in a DC generator.

altimeter.note: Reading height off the pressure, and being wrong when the weather changes.

ambulance.note: A vehicle built round a stretcher and the things needed on the way.

amphitheatre.note: An oval of seating raised on its own vaults, so the crowd walks in underneath.

and_gate.note: On only when both inputs are.

anemometer.note: Cups catch the wind and spin a shaft; the rotation rate is the wind speed.

antiseptic_dressing.note: Cotton soaked in carbolic acid, packed onto a wound — Lister's method halved surgical deaths.

anvil.note: Mass under the hammer, so the blow goes into the work and not the floor.

apache_helicopter.note: Its Longbow radar, mounted above the rotor, tracks targets while the helicopter hides behind terrain.

aperture.note: A hole you can change the size of, which controls both light and what is sharp.

apollo_11.note: Three vehicles, two of which were thrown away, and the third came home.

aqueduct.note: Gravity does all the work, so the fall is a component: a few centimetres per kilometre, held unbroken over tens of kilometres.

arch.note: Wedges that cannot fall because there is nowhere for them to go.

archimedes_screw.note: A helix in a tube — turning it lifts pockets of water without valves or suction.

arena.note: The floor of the fight, sanded so it can be raked clean between events.

armature.note: The winding that the current does its work in.

armet.note: The first helmet that genuinely closes, with cheekpieces that hinge shut.

arrow.note: A shaft stiff enough for the bow that shoots it, weighted at the front and steered at the back.

artificial_heart.note: Power crosses the skin by magnetic induction — no wire, so no infection path.

astronaut.note: A person trained for an environment that will kill them in seconds.

atlatl.note: A lever that adds a joint to the arm, doubling the dart's speed.

atomic_clock.note: The quartz oscillator does the timekeeping; the atoms only correct it. The clock is a servo loop, not a resonator.

autogyro.note: The rotor is not powered — air flowing up through it as the craft moves forward makes it spin.

axle.note: A shaft that carries the wheel, and the surfaces it turns on.

backrest.note: The part that decides whether a chair can be sat in for an hour.

baffle.note: A plate in the way, so the flow cannot go straight.

bagpipes.note: The bag feeds reed pipes so the player can breathe while the drone continues.

balance.note: A beam, a pivot, and two pans — and it measures mass rather than weight.

balance_wheel.note: A wheel and a hairspring, oscillating at a rate that does not care about the mainspring.

banknote_pound.note: A promise printed so well that copying it costs more than it is worth.

barbute.note: A single-piece Italian skull with a T-shaped opening, the shape deliberately echoing ancient Greek helmets.

barometer.note: A column of mercury the atmosphere is holding up, or a sealed box it is squeezing.

barrel.note: Curved staves squeezed into a shape that holds itself together.

basilica.note: A long hall with aisles and a clerestory, built for business and borrowed by the church.

basket.note: Rods for the frame, weavers for the skin.

bassoon.note: Eight feet of conical bore folded in half so a person can hold it.

bastion_fort.note: Low and thick rather than tall, because the point is to absorb round shot instead of standing over it, and every face has to be covered by fire from another face.

battery.note: Two different metals and something that will carry ions between them.

beam.note: A member loaded across its length — deepest where the bending is worst.

bearing.note: Two rings, rolling elements between them, and a cage to keep those elements apart — which is the part people forget and the part that decides its life.

bell.note: A casting whose profile is tuned by turning metal off the inside.

bifocals.note: Two lenses' halves set in one frame — near vision below, distance above. Franklin, 1784.

bionic_arm.note: Targeted muscle reinnervation lets the brain's old nerve signals drive the new hand.

black_hawk.note: Two engines where its predecessor had one — designed to survive a single engine failure.

blade.note: A wedge, and a heat treatment that makes the wedge stay a wedge.

block.note: Pulleys in a shell, and each rope in the system takes a share.

block_signal.note: The train itself closes the circuit — a wheel and axle short the rails.

boat.note: A shell that keeps water out, stiffened inside, with something to drive and steer it.

bob.note: The weight at the bottom, and moving it is how the clock is set.

body_panel.note: Sheet steel pressed into a shape that is stiffer than the sheet.

boiler.note: Pressure builds where fire meets water — the safety valve is the difference between power and explosion.

bolt.note: A threaded pin that clamps by being stretched.

bombe.note: A machine that ran Enigma settings until one did not contradict itself.

bone_rongeur.note: Spring-loaded steel jaws that gnaw bone away chip by chip.

book.note: A codex is folded sheets sewn in gatherings, which is why it opens flat and a scroll does not.

boot.note: A shoe that keeps going past the ankle, which is a structural decision.

bosra.note: A theatre so completely swallowed by a later fortress that it survived intact inside it.

bow.note: A stave that stores energy, and a string that releases it.

bow_drill.note: A bow turns hand-spinning into a back-and-forth that doesn't tire the wrists.

bradley_ifv.note: A troop carrier armed like a light tank — it fights, not just delivers.

brake.note: Turning motion into heat, and then getting rid of the heat.

brake_disc.note: A steel plate that has to take the heat and stay flat.

brake_pad.note: Friction material on a steel backing, chosen to wear instead of the disc.

brick.note: Clay, water, a shape, and enough heat to make the change permanent.

broom.note: Stiff fibre bound to a handle, and the binding is what wears out.

bucket.note: A cooper's trade scaled down — staves bent and hooped, or pressed steel after galvanising.

bulk_carrier.note: Capesize ships too big for canals carry 75% of the world's iron ore by sea.

burgonet.note: An open helmet with a peak and a comb, for people who had to see.

cabin.note: The part designed around the people rather than the machine.

caboose.note: The cupola let the crew watch the whole train for shifted loads or hotboxes.

cache.note: Keeping the answer nearby because you will be asked again.

caisson.note: Men work in compressed air below the water table; the bends killed many before decompression was understood.

caliper.note: The clamp that squeezes the pads onto the disc.

cam.note: A shaped disc that makes a follower move to a plan you drew.

camshaft.note: A shaft with the engine's whole timing carved into it.

canal_lock.note: A boat lift with no machinery: two gates, two paddles, and the water does the lifting.

candle.note: A fuel that melts before it burns, and a wick that draws it up.

canned_heat.note: Fuel held in a gel so it burns where it is put.

cannon.note: A tube strong enough to survive what happens inside it, on something that absorbs the recoil.

canoe.note: The first boats were hollowed logs; bark and skin versions traded weight for the need for a frame.

canvas.note: A plain weave heavy enough to take tension without stretching out of shape.

capacitor.note: Two plates that never touch, and something between them that will not conduct.

capstone.note: The stone on top, and often the one that makes the rest work.

carbon_fibre.note: A polymer filament cooked until only carbon is left.

carburettor.note: Air rushing through a narrowing drags fuel in behind it, and the ratio is geometry.

cargo.note: Whatever the ship is actually for.

carriage.note: A body slung on springs above wheels, so the road is not transmitted to the passenger.

cask.note: Staves sprung into hoops — watertight without glue.

cassini_huygens.note: An orbiter and a lander, and the lander went to a moon with weather.

catalytic_converter.note: The washcoat roughens the surface so a tiny amount of platinum does the work of a solid lump.

cavity_wall_tie.note: A twist of steel holding two leaves apart and together at once.

cd.note: A pit in the aluminium layer shortens the reflected pulse — that's all a bit is.

ceiling.note: A grid hung below the structure, hiding the pipes and wires that live in the plenum.

cello.note: Tuned an octave below the viola; the endpin that lets the player sit appeared only in the 1840s.

centrifugal_governor.note: Spinning flyweights swing outward as speed rises and choke the throttle — negative feedback in iron.

ch47_chinook.note: Two counter-rotating rotors cancel torque — no tail rotor needed.

chain.note: Links, and the weld that makes a link a link.

chassis.note: The frame everything is bolted to, and what decides how the car behaves.

cheese.note: Separate the curd from the whey, then decide how long you can wait.

chisel.note: A hardened wedge on a shaft you can hit.

choke.note: Deliberately starving the engine of air, because a cold one needs more fuel.

church.note: A room laid out so a crowd can face one end and hear what happens there.

circuit_board.note: The copper is etched away to leave tracks; the substrate is fibreglass with epoxy resin.

city.note: A settlement too large to feed itself, so the surrounding farmland is a component of the city as much as its walls are.

clapper.note: The bit that hits, and it has to strike and then get out of the way.

clasp.note: The deliberate weak point where a closed loop can be opened.

clock.note: A source of power, something that counts, and something that stops the counting from running away.

close_helmet.note: A helmet that closes completely round the head and pivots on one axis.

cloth.note: Fibre, spun, then crossed at right angles under tension.

clutch.note: Two spinning things brought together gently enough not to break anything.

coating.note: A layer added for a property the thing underneath does not have.

cockpit.note: Everything the pilot has to reach, arranged so it can be reached without looking.

coil.note: Wire turned round enough times that a small current makes a large field.

coin.note: A weighed blank and two dies struck together.

column.note: A vertical in pure compression, and the failure mode is buckling not crushing.

compass.note: A magnet free to turn, and everything else is keeping it free.

compiler.note: Turning something a person wrote into something a processor will run.

composing_stick.note: Where a line of type is assembled, backwards and upside down.

composite_bow.note: Horn on the belly for compression, sinew on the back for tension, wood between them holding the two apart — and a year or more of glue drying between steps.

computer_mouse.note: Turning a hand's movement into two numbers.

concentric_castle.note: The inner wall is higher so both can fire at once, and the narrow space between them is a killing ground.

concrete.note: Cement is the glue, aggregate is the bulk, water is the reaction; steel is what stops it failing in tension.

condenser.note: Taking a vapour back to a liquid by taking its heat away.

confocal_microscope.note: A pinhole rejects light from every plane except one, so stacked slices build a 3D image.

contact_tracing.note: Following an infection backwards and forwards through the people it touched.

contagion.note: Disease moving from one person to the next, and what has to be true for it to.

continuous_miner.note: A rotating drum rips coal off the face, replacing separate cutting, drilling, and blasting.

coolant.note: A liquid that carries heat away and does not freeze, boil or corrode on the way.

corbel_vault.note: Each course stepped inward until the gap closes. No wedge, no thrust, no arch.

counterweight.note: Mass on the other side, so the machine lifts the load and not itself.

coupler.note: Push two cars together and the knuckle locks itself — no one stands between them.

crane.note: Lifting is easy; not falling over is the engineering.

crank.note: Turning rotation into a push and back again, which is most of the industrial revolution.

credit.note: Being trusted with money you have not got yet.

crown.note: Precious metal, worked thin, made to be seen from a distance.

crypt.note: A vaulted room under the floor, which is also what holds the floor up.

ct_scanner.note: An X-ray tube and detectors spin around the patient; a computer stacks the slices into a volume.

culvert.note: A pipe under a road, sized for the flood and not the stream.

currency.note: Money a state says is money, and enforces.

curtain_wall.note: It carries only its own weight and the wind. Everything holding the building up is behind it.

dashboard.note: The instruments, and the structure that stops them arriving in your lap.

data_bus.note: The shared wiring everything inside a computer talks over.

database.note: Storing facts so they can be found again, and not lost when the power goes.

debakey_forceps.note: Fine ridges grip vessels without crushing — the atraumatic pattern.

debt.note: A promise to pay later, priced by how likely you are to.

deck.note: The horizontal that ties a hull's sides together and stops it folding.

diagnosis.note: Working out which condition explains what is in front of you.

diaper.note: Three layers: a wicking topsheet, absorbent core, and waterproof backsheet.

diesel_electric_locomotive.note: The diesel engine never touches the wheels — it spins a generator that feeds traction motors.

differential.note: The spider gears walk around when one wheel slips, splitting the torque evenly even when the speeds differ.

dilator.note: A graduated series, each wider than the last, stretches tissue slowly.

disease.note: A process that makes a body work worse, and can be named.

disorder.note: A pattern of distress or impairment a clinician has agreed to name.

distillation.note: Boiling a mixture and catching the part that leaves first.

djembe.note: Carved from one log while the wood is still green.

djemila.note: A Roman town that had to bend its own street grid because the ridge would not take one.

doctor.note: Somebody licensed to decide what is wrong and what to do.

dollar.note: A unit of account, and the thing everyone else prices against.

domain_name_system.note: Turning a name into an address, in a hierarchy nobody owns all of.

dome.note: A shell in compression, and a way to stop it spreading at the bottom.

door.note: A panel, a way to hang it, and a way to hold it shut.

dose.note: How much, how often, and for how long.

dragline_excavator.note: The bucket hangs from a boom on two ropes — one hoists, one drags — reaching 100 metres or more.

driveshaft.note: A tube that must carry torque while both ends move relative to each other.

drone.note: Two rotors spin clockwise and two anticlockwise, so the torques cancel.

drug.note: A molecule chosen because of what it does to a target.

drum.note: A membrane held under tension over an opening.

dvd_player.note: A laser reads a spiral of pits by interference; the disc spins faster as the head moves inward.

earthwork.note: Moving soil, and the spoil from the ditch becomes the bank.

echo_sounder.note: Times a ping's round trip to the seafloor, which needs knowing the speed of sound in water at that depth.

economy.note: Everything people make, move and exchange, counted.

ectfe.note: A copolymer chosen for chemical resistance and a surface nothing sticks to.

electric_car.note: No engine, no gearbox, no idle — the motor delivers full torque from zero rpm.

electric_locomotive.note: No engine on board — current from an overhead wire or third rail drives the motors directly.

electric_motor.note: A field, a rotor in it, and a way to keep pushing the rotor the same way round.

elephant_clock.note: A sinking float trips a see-saw every half hour, dropping a ball to strike a drummer atop an elephant.

elevator.note: The governor trips the safety brake the instant the car overspeeds.

embankment.note: An earth dam holds by weight and by not letting water through the middle.

epdm.note: A rubber with no double bonds in the backbone, so ozone and sunlight leave it alone.

epidemiology.note: Counting who gets ill, where, and why.

escapement.note: Letting the gear train move one step at a time, and keeping the pendulum going while it does.

ethylene_glycol.note: An antifreeze that tastes sweet, which is the whole problem with it.

extruder.note: A screw in a heated barrel, pushing a melt through a shaped die.

eyepiece.note: The second lens, and the one that decides what the eye is actually shown.

fastener.note: Anything that holds two things together and comes apart again.

feast.note: Cooking for more people than the kitchen was built for.

feed_dog.note: The teeth under the needle plate that move the cloth one stitch at a time.

felt.note: Wool, water, heat and pressure — no thread anywhere in it.

ferrari.note: A road car built by a company that made road cars to pay for racing.

festival.note: A day the calendar sets aside, and everything that has to be arranged for it.

filesystem.note: Turning a flat expanse of blocks into names and folders.

film.note: The antihalation layer absorbs light that would otherwise bounce back through the emulsion and blur the image.

fin.note: A surface that keeps something pointing the way it is going.

firebox.note: Copper inside, steel outside, and stay bolts holding them together under pressure.

firefighter.note: Someone who goes toward it, carrying their own air.

fixative.note: Something that evaporates slowly, so the fast things do not all leave at once.

fkm.note: A rubber that survives fuel and heat, which ordinary rubber does not.

flanged_mace.note: Flanges brazed to the head bite into plate armor instead of glancing off.

flintlock_musket.note: Flint struck steel to spark the priming pan — more reliable than matchlock, simpler than wheellock.

flip_flop.note: Two gates feeding each other, so the circuit remembers.

flying_buttress.note: A half-arch standing away from the wall, and the pinnacle on top of the pier is structural: its weight turns the thrust downward into the pier.

flying_shuttle.note: Kay's 1733 shuttle ran on wheels, so one weaver could work cloth wider than an arm's reach.

flyssa.note: A narrow single-edged Algerian blade of the Kabyle, capped with a distinctive T-shaped pommel.

flyweight.note: Weights that fly outward as the speed rises, and pull a lever as they go.

flywheel.note: Storing rotation, so the machine keeps going between pushes.

foam.note: Gas held in a solid, so a little material fills a lot of space.

font.note: A set of shapes designed to be read rather than looked at.

forbidden_city.note: 980 buildings on one axis, with the roof colour telling you the rank.

forge.note: Fire, air, and a way to hold what you are heating.

fork_garden.note: Tines instead of a blade, because clay will not let a spade out again.

formwork.note: The mould you build, fill, and then take away.

forum.note: The open square everything civic faced onto.

fragrance.note: Top, heart and base notes, which is really three evaporation rates.

frame.note: Members that carry load, and joints that stop them folding.

fridge.note: Moving heat out of a box, which takes work, which is why the back is warm.

fuel_cell.note: Combines hydrogen and oxygen without burning, making electricity, heat, and water.

fuel_tank.note: A sealed vessel that must breathe without spilling and not slosh.

furnace.note: A box that holds heat in and air through: lining, shell, a way to force air, and a way to let gas out.

galalith.note: Milk protein and formaldehyde — a plastic made from cheese.

galleon.note: The high stern gave archers and musketeers a platform when boarded; the low bow let the bow chasers fire forward.

gambeson.note: Quilted armour that works by trapping air in pockets — padding that could stop a blow by itself.

gate.note: The deliberate weak point in a barrier, so it gets more ironwork per square metre than the wall it interrupts.

gauntlet.note: Overlapping steel plates riveted over a leather glove — a stiff mitten or articulated fingers.

generator.note: Faraday's law made into hardware: a magnetic field, a conductor, and relative motion between them.

germicidal_uv.note: UV-C at 254 nm welds a microbe's DNA bases together in pairs that cannot replicate.

gigli_saw.note: A twisted-wire saw thin enough to slip under the skull.

glass.note: The soda-lime batch that is 90% of all glass made, plus what it takes to melt and shape it.

glasses.note: Two lenses held before the eyes — temples over the ears took four centuries after the lens itself.

goal.note: Football had no net until 1889 — the net is what settles an argument.

gong.note: A bronze disc quenched from red heat so it can be hammered soft.

governor.note: A machine that measures its own speed and does something about it.

granary.note: Dry, off the ground, and shut against everything that also eats grain.

great_house.note: Pueblo Bonito had 600+ rooms in a single planned build — nothing that size was built north of Mexico for another 800 years.

greenhouse.note: It works by stopping warm air rising away rather than by trapping infrared, which is the opposite of what the name has come to mean in climate.

gyroscope.note: The gimbal lets the rotor point wherever it wants; the bearing lets it spin.

halberd.note: Three weapons on one shaft — an axe to cut, a spike to thrust, and a hook to pull riders down.

half_adder.note: Two bits in, a sum and a carry out.

hammer.note: A heavy head and a handle long enough to swing it — and an eye that keeps the two together.

handlebar.note: Where steering, braking, shifting and most of the weight all meet.

harbour.note: Somewhere the sea stops being weather.

harmonica.note: One reed set sounds on the blow, another on the draw.

harness.note: Distributes the pull from collar to traces without pressing the windpipe.

harp.note: Strings rise nearly perpendicular from the soundboard, which is what gives the harp its shape.

heat_exchanger.note: Two fluids swapping heat without meeting.

heat_shield.note: Survives re-entry by being destroyed slowly — ablation carries the heat away.

heat_sink.note: Getting heat out of something small into something large.

helicopter.note: The swashplate is the whole trick: it turns a stationary control input into a blade angle that changes once per revolution.

hellfire_missile.note: Homes on a laser spot someone else paints, not the launch aircraft.

helmet.note: A hard shell that does not touch the head, and a liner that keeps it that way.

hemostat.note: Kocher's ratchet locks the clamp shut with no hand holding it.

hepa_filter.note: Certified to trap 99.97% of particles at 0.3 micrometres — the size that slips through most easily.

highlighter.note: Ink you can read through, which is the whole trick.

hilt.note: Everything on a sword that is not the blade: the guard stops the hand sliding onto the edge.

himars.note: The same launcher as the M270, but with one pod on a truck instead of two on tracks.

hinge.note: Two leaves, a knuckle each, and one pin through both. Everything else is finish.

hmmwv.note: Portal axles let the drivetrain sit above the wheel centers, nearly doubling ground clearance without raising the body.

hoe.note: A blade at an angle to a handle, for cutting weeds below the surface.

hose.note: The reinforcement is what keeps it round under pressure; the rubber only keeps the water in.

house.note: A builder's list, in the order the site works: ground, structure, envelope, services, finish.

housing.note: The case that keeps the bearings aligned and everything else out.

hubble_space_telescope.note: A telescope above the air, and a mirror ground precisely to the wrong shape.

hull.note: Planks are the skin, frames are the skeleton, and the keel is the spine — carvel or clinker decides how they meet.

hydroelectric_dam.note: Water drops through a penstock into a turbine — a whole river's fall, spent in one place.

hydrogen_bomb.note: Two stages in one case: the first is a fission bomb used only as a match, and the case itself is a component because it holds the radiation in long enough to compress the second.

hygrometer.note: Human hair lengthens as humidity rises — De Saussure's 1783 design still works.

icbm.note: Most of the flight is a fall, which is what ballistic means.

icebreaker.note: The hull bends and breaks ice by riding up onto it, not ramming.

incineration.note: Burning waste hot enough that what comes out is not worse.

inductor.note: A coil that resists a change in current, because a changing field pushes back.

ink.note: A colourant, something to carry it, and something to make it stay.

innate_immunity.note: The defences that are already there before anything has been learned.

insole.note: The layer between the foot and everything the shoe is made of.

international_space_station.note: Modules launched separately over decades and bolted together in orbit.

internet.note: Not one network but many agreeing to forward each other's packets, so the routing protocol is as much a component as the cable.

jacquard_loom.note: The punched card was the first mass storage — one card per row of the design.

javelin_missile.note: Fire-and-forget — the gunner can take cover while the missile guides itself.

jpeg.note: Throwing away what the eye does not notice, on purpose.

katana.note: Differentially tempered — the edge is harder than the spine, and the curve comes from quenching.

katar.note: The H-grip puts the blade in line with the forearm — a punch lands the whole arm's weight.

katzbalger.note: A short, sturdy sword with a distinctive S-shaped guard, the Landsknecht's backup weapon.

kevlar.note: Rod-like molecules aligned along the fibre, hydrogen-bonded to their neighbours.

kiln.note: A box that gets hot enough and cools slowly enough, and the second half is what breaks the pot.

kilwa_kisiwani.note: A Swahili trading city built in coral, that controlled the Zimbabwe gold trade.

kiowa_warrior.note: The mast-mounted sight lets it observe from behind cover with just the sensor ball exposed.

kite.note: The bridle sets the angle of attack; wrong and the kite dives or will not lift.

knife.note: A hard edge on a tough spine, and a handle that will not come off.

kris.note: Pattern-welded from layered iron and nickel iron — the wavy blade is ritual as much as weapon.

laryngoscope.note: Macintosh's curve lifts the epiglottis indirectly to spare the teeth.

laser.note: A gain medium between two mirrors, and something to pump energy into it. One mirror is deliberately imperfect, and the light that leaks through it is the beam.

lathe.note: The machine that makes machines: it turns the work and holds the cutter still, and a lathe is the only tool that can build its own successor.

ldpe.note: Branched chains that cannot pack, so it is soft, clear and floppy.

leather.note: A hide stopped from rotting, then made soft again.

led.note: Electrons fall into holes; the gap size sets the colour.

leg.note: A vertical member under a horizontal one, and the joint is the whole problem.

lever.note: A rigid bar, a fulcrum, and the choice of where to put it.

light_bulb.note: A wire hot enough to glow, in an atmosphere that will not let it burn.

lightning_rod.note: A grounded iron point gives a stroke somewhere safe to go instead of the building. Franklin, 1752.

limousine.note: A car cut in half and lengthened, with the join done properly.

liquid_fuel_rocket.note: Two tanks, two pumps and a chamber, and the pumps are the hard part.

litter.note: Rubbish outside the system that was built to contain it.

load.note: What a structure has to hold up, including itself.

lock.note: Something that will not move until the right shape moves it.

log_building.note: The corner notch is everything: a dovetail notch sheds water; a saddle notch collects it.

logic_gate.note: A switch made of switches, and the whole of computing sits on it.

longbow.note: The stave is cut so heartwood is on the belly and sapwood on the back: one resists compression, the other tension, and it is a natural composite in a single piece.

longship.note: Clinker-built: each plank overlaps the one below and is riveted through, so the hull flexes with the sea instead of resisting it.

longwall_shearer.note: Twin drums shear coal off the face as the shearer rides the conveyor back and forth.

loom.note: Every loom does the same four things in the same order, and everything else is speed.

lyre.note: A soundbox, two arms, a crossbar, and strings you can tune.

m109_paladin.note: A self-propelled howitzer that can fire and move before the shells land.

m249_saw.note: Belt-fed but fires the same round as the squad's rifles.

m2_browning.note: Browning's 1918 design still in production a century later.

machine.note: Anything that changes a force or a motion into a different one.

macuahuitl.note: Obsidian blades sharper than steel, but brittle — they shatter on armor.

madrasah.note: Four iwans round a courtyard, with the students living in the walls.

magill_forceps.note: The angle lets you guide a tube past the vocal cords under direct vision.

magnet.note: Domains lined up, and something to stop them wandering back.

magnetising_coil.note: A brief, enormous current aligns the domains permanently in one pulse.

main_gauche.note: A parrying dagger for the off hand, its ring-guard curved to trap an opponent's blade.

malbork.note: The largest brick castle in the world, built as a headquarters rather than a fortress.

mammoth_bone_hut.note: A dome of bones and tusks on treeless steppe, where mammoth skeletons were the only building material.

maximilian_armor.note: Steel hammered into close-set parallel flutes for rigidity without extra weight.

mbira.note: Tuned metal tongues plucked with the thumbs, over a resonator that is meant to buzz.

mechanism.note: The linkage — the part that decides what moves when something else does.

medicine.note: The whole enterprise of finding out what is wrong and doing something about it.

megalith.note: Stones too big to lift, moved anyway.

metal_detector.note: Two induction coils balance against each other until metal nearby throws the field off.

metronidazole.note: A drug that only becomes a poison inside things that live without oxygen.

microphone.note: The diaphragm's motion becomes an electrical signal — dynamic mics use a coil in a magnetic field.

microprocessor.note: Millions of transistors printed at once, and the wiring between them.

microscope.note: Two lenses in series, and a great deal of trouble getting light through the specimen.

microwave_oven.note: Spencer's 1946 accident: a radar magnetron melted a chocolate bar in his pocket.

millstone.note: A pair of dressed stones, the upper turning on the lower; the furrows throw flour to the edge.

mirror.note: A flat, clean sheet and a metal film behind it.

missile.note: Something that steers itself at a thing that is moving.

mlrs.note: A tracked launcher that fires twelve rockets in under a minute, and everything required to reload it in the field.

moat.note: A ditch that either holds water or is not worth digging.

modem.note: Turning bits into a sound a phone line will carry, and back.

money.note: A thing everyone will accept, so trade no longer needs both sides to want.

monitor.note: A grid of cells that can be told what colour to be, sixty times a second.

morin_khuur.note: Strings and bow both traditionally horsehair.

morion.note: A high comb and a swept brim, and the comb is structural.

mosque.note: The mihrab niche points the qibla; the minbar lets the imam be heard.

motherboard.note: A board whose job is entirely connection: everything on it is there to let the other things talk.

motor.note: Anything that turns because a field is pulling it round.

motorcycle.note: A bicycle with an engine, and everything that had to change once it had one.

motte_and_bailey.note: A mound, a ditch, and timber palisades — quick to build with unskilled labour.

mrap_vehicle.note: The V-hull throws blast sideways instead of straight up through the floor.

multiplexer.note: Choosing one of several inputs with a switch made of gates.

nabataean.note: A people who got rich on incense and survived on water nobody else could find.

naginata.note: A curved blade on a pole — used to dismount cavalry and keep infantry at distance.

nand_gate.note: The one gate you can build every other gate out of.

nave.note: The long hall the congregation stands in, and the reason a basilica is shaped like that.

necklace.note: What actually goes into one, across the whole range — a strand of pierced shells and a set diamond on a gold chain are the same object doing the same job.

needle.note: A point, a shaft stiff enough not to bend, and an eye that does not weaken it.

needle_holder.note: Tungsten carbide jaws grip the needle without slipping or spinning.

needle_valve.note: The long taper gives fine control — a large turn for a small change in flow.

neoprene.note: Synthetic rubber full of closed gas cells, which is what a wetsuit is.

newgrange.note: A passage tomb with a roof box aligned so the midwinter sun reaches the back.

nike_plus_sensor.note: A piezoelectric pad under the insole counts steps and radios the count to the player.

not_gate.note: One transistor and a resistor, and it is the whole of negation.

nuclear_power_plant.note: The reactor never spins anything itself — it just boils water for a turbine.

nuclear_reactor.note: Control rods and moderator are both components, and they do opposite jobs: one slows the neutrons so the reaction can happen, the other swallows them so it does not run away.

nurdle.note: The pellet everything plastic is shipped as, and the reason it is on every beach.

nurse.note: The trade that is with the patient when nobody else is.

nylon.note: A polyamide with the same hydrogen bonding that makes silk strong.

oar.note: A lever whose fulcrum is the boat, not the water.

ocean_liner.note: Watertight bulkheads split the hull — Titanic's simply didn't go high enough.

oldowan_tool.note: The oldest stone tools: sharp flakes struck off a core with a hammerstone, 2.6 million years ago.

operating_system.note: Everything between the metal and the program, and almost all of it is about sharing.

oriflamme.note: Red silk on a gilded lance — France's sacred battle standard.

outbreak.note: More cases than expected, in one place, at one time.

oxo_degradable_plastic.note: Plastic with a salt added so it breaks into pieces rather than breaking down.

pagoda.note: The storeys are stacked rather than tied, and the central pillar hangs rather than carries — which is why they survive earthquakes that flatten what is around them.

paint.note: Pigment carried in a binder, thinned to spread and left to harden.

panel.note: A board floating in a groove, free to move as the wood changes size.

paper.note: Fibre, water, a screen to catch it on, and pressure to take the water out.

parchment.note: Skin that was never tanned — limed, stretched, and dried under tension.

patient.note: The person all of this is supposed to be for.

patriot_missile.note: Its phased-array radar tracks both target and missile, radioing course corrections.

pedal.note: Where a foot meets a machine, and where the bearings live a hard life.

peeler.note: The slot in the blade lets the edge rock, taking off a thin strip no matter how the hand tilts.

pendentive.note: The curved triangle that lets a round dome sit on a square room. Without it a dome needs a round wall under it.

pendulum.note: A period that depends on length and gravity and almost nothing else.

perfume.note: Three evaporation rates, arranged so a scent unfolds over hours.

pergamon.note: A city terraced up a 335 m cone, so every building stands on a retaining wall.

pesto.note: Pounded rather than chopped, because a blade bruises basil and a stone does not.

pet.note: Clear, tough, and the only common plastic that is genuinely recycled at scale.

petrol.note: A blend, not a compound — tuned so it burns when it is told to and not before.

phase_contrast_microscope.note: An annular ring and a phase plate turn invisible phase shifts into visible brightness differences.

phonograph_record.note: A stamped copy of a groove that was once cut by a stylus moving to sound.

phosphor.note: A material that takes in one colour of light and gives out another, slowly.

piano_action.note: Fifty-odd parts per key, so that a finger can throw a hammer and let it fall back.

pickaxe.note: Concentrating a swing onto a point, which is how rock is beaten rather than cut.

pickup.note: A cab and an open bed on one frame.

pilum.note: The soft iron shank is a feature, not a flaw: it bends on impact so the javelin cannot be thrown back and drags on any shield it pierces.

pingyao.note: A Ming walled city that kept its plan because it got poor at the right moment.

pipe.note: A tube, a way to join tubes, and a way to stop the join leaking.

pistol.note: A wheellock handgun short enough to fire one-handed and hide under a cloak.

plaster.note: A powder that sets when you wet it, on something for it to hold to.

plastic.note: A long molecule that can be melted, moulded, and will not go away.

plastic_recycling.note: Sorting, washing, shredding and remelting — and losing a little quality each time.

plate_armor.note: Shaped plates that overlap so the joints move and the gaps do not line up.

platen.note: The flat that presses the paper onto the type, evenly or not at all.

pliers.note: Two levers crossed on a pivot — the jaws grip while the handles stay apart.

plough.note: Cut it, lift it, turn it over. Three jobs, three parts, and the mouldboard is the one that changed farming.

plug_bayonet.note: A blade with a tapered handle that jams in the muzzle, which stops the gun firing.

plumbing.note: Water in under pressure, out under gravity, and the trap between them.

podium.note: The wall between the crowd and whatever is on the sand.

polyester.note: Two chemicals condensing into a chain, then melted and squirted into fibre.

polyethylene.note: The simplest polymer there is, and the most of it.

polyisoprene.note: The molecule natural rubber is, made in a reactor instead of a tree.

polyurethane.note: Two liquids that become a solid the moment they meet.

portcullis.note: The lattice drops into grooves in the jambs, trapping attackers between two of them.

pot.note: Clay, a way to make it round, and fire.

power_grid.note: Generation and consumption must stay balanced — energy is consumed as it is made.

press.note: Force applied slowly and exactly where it is wanted.

proof_armor.note: A breastplate shot with a pistol on purpose — the dent left behind was the proof mark.

pula_arena.note: The only Roman amphitheatre with all four side towers still standing.

pulley.note: Each extra line halves the force and doubles the distance; the work is unchanged but the rope is longer.

pump.note: A chamber that changes volume and two valves that only let water go one way.

pvc.note: The polymer that is rigid or floppy depending entirely on what is added to it.

pvdf.note: A fluoropolymer that is also piezoelectric, which almost nothing else is.

pyrolysis.note: Heating something apart without letting it burn.

quenching_trough.note: A tank of the right liquid at the right temperature, beside the fire.

race.note: Everybody going the same way at once, timed.

radiator.note: Most of the heat leaves by convection; the radiator name stuck from when they were cast iron and radiated more.

rain_gauge.note: A funnel over a cylinder. Korea's cheugugi, standardised in 1441, was the world's first.

rake.note: Tines spaced so soil passes and stones do not.

read_only_memory.note: The pattern is fixed at fabrication, which is why the data survives the power going off.

rebar.note: Steel where the concrete is in tension, which concrete cannot do.

receiver.note: Picking one signal out of everything arriving at the antenna.

recombinant_dna.note: Cutting DNA at a known place and pasting somebody else's in.

reed_organ.note: No pipes at all — foot-pumped bellows drive free reeds.

reflecting_telescope.note: A mirror instead of a lens, so colour does not smear and size is not limited by glass.

reflector.note: Sending light back exactly the way it came, whatever angle it arrived at.

register.note: The handful of places a processor can hold a number without going anywhere.

repeating_crossbow.note: A gravity-fed magazine of bolts, worked by one lever — faster but weaker than a hand-drawn crossbow.

reservoir.note: Holding water back so that it is there when the rain is not.

resistor.note: The value is set by the material and the geometry — carbon, wire, or film.

rivet.note: A pin with a head, given a second head after it is through.

road.note: Layers, each one spreading the load over more of the one beneath.

robotic_arm.note: Joints in series, and the error at the end is every joint's error added together.

rocket.note: Throwing mass backwards hard enough to go the other way.

rod.note: A long solid section, loaded along its length or across it.

roman_forum.note: A market square that became the centre of an empire and then a cow pasture.

roof.note: A frame that sheds water, and a skin that does not let it in.

rootstock.note: The bottom half of a grafted plant, chosen for the soil rather than the fruit.

rope.note: Fibre into yarn, yarn into strand, strand into rope — each layer twisted against the one below so it cannot unlay.

rubbish.note: What is left when nobody will pay to keep it in circulation.

ruler.note: A straight edge with the units already on it.

runway_deicer.note: Lowering the freezing point of water on a surface that cannot be salted.

sagalassos.note: A mountain city abandoned after an earthquake and never built over.

sallet.note: A helmet with a long tail, worn with a bevor because it leaves the chin open.

saltire.note: A diagonal cross, and one of the oldest heraldic charges there is.

sandalwood_tree.note: A tree that cannot feed itself and taps the roots of its neighbours.

sash.note: The frame that holds the glass and slides while the frame around it does not.

saw.note: The teeth are bent alternately left and right, so the cut is wider than the blade and the blade does not bind.

scabbard.note: The throat keeps the edge from cutting its own sheath; the chape takes the wear.

scaffold.note: A temporary frame of tubes and boards that puts a working platform where the building is not finished yet.

scanning_electron_microscope.note: A beam scans the surface, and the scattered electrons build a 3D-looking image.

scanning_tunneling_microscope.note: A sharp tip within angstroms of a surface — electrons tunnel across a gap they classically shouldn't.

schiavona.note: A basket hilt of leaf-shaped iron bars fully enclosing the hand, named for Slavic mercenaries who carried it.

scimitar.note: A light, curved slashing sword optimized for mounted combat.

screen.note: A grid of things that can be made to glow or not.

seat.note: Somewhere to put a person, at a height and an angle that has been thought about.

seatbelt.note: Webbing, a reel that locks, and an anchor strong enough to matter.

sector.note: One slice of an economy, defined by how far it is from the raw material.

sedan.note: Three boxes — engine, people, luggage — and the middle one is the point.

seismograph.note: A mass too lazy to move while its frame shakes — the difference is the measurement.

serration.note: Teeth on an edge, so it saws where a plain edge would slide.

sewer.note: Getting waste away under gravity, and stopping it coming back.

sewing_machine.note: The lockstitch needs two threads that never pass through each other, which is why the needle has its eye at the point.

sextant.note: It measures the angle between two things, which is why it works on a moving deck when nothing else does.

shackle.note: A U of metal with a removable pin, so two things can be joined and unjoined.

shaft_rotating.note: A round bar carrying torque, and the failure is always torsion at a step.

shampoo.note: A detergent mild enough for skin, plus everything undoing what the detergent did.

shamshir.note: A Persian saber curved into a radical arc — the name literally means 'lion's claw'.

shicra.note: Bags of stone, stacked — a building technique and possibly an earthquake damper.

shock_absorber.note: A spring stores the bump; this is what stops it giving it back.

shotel.note: Curved to reach around a shield — the hook can catch a shoulder or pull the shield aside.

shutter.note: Blades that open and close fast enough to freeze motion, and a mechanism that times them.

sickle.note: A curved edge that cuts by drawing, and a handle set to keep the wrist straight.

silk.note: One continuous filament, unwound rather than spun.

silo.note: What goes in as grain comes out as feed — fermentation under exclusion of air.

sim_card.note: A chip that proves which subscriber you are, in a card small enough to move.

single_use_plastic.note: Made to be thrown away, and made of something that will not go.

sitar.note: The sympathetic strings vibrate untouched, adding shimmer.

skyscraper.note: The core takes the load; the glass skin merely keeps the weather out.

sling.note: A pouch on two cords, whirled overhead — one cord releases and the stone flies.

smallsword.note: A light triangular-bladed sword for the thrust alone — no 18th-century gentleman was dressed without one.

snow_groomer.note: A tracked tiller combs the piste into corduroy, winched up the steepest pitches.

soap.note: One reaction, known for four thousand years: fat and a strong alkali.

socket.note: A cup that grips a hexagon on six faces instead of two.

socket_bayonet.note: A blade that fits round the barrel rather than in it, so the gun still fires.

sorghum_broomcorn.note: A grass grown for its seed head rather than its seed.

soundboard.note: Spruce is preferred for its high stiffness-to-weight ratio; bracing controls how it flexes.

spade.note: A flat blade for cutting into ground, with a step to take the boot.

spandex.note: Rigid blocks holding coiled ones, so it stretches and goes back.

spark_plug.note: The insulator keeps 40,000 volts from jumping anywhere but the gap.

spatula.note: A flat blade with enough spring to get under something and not through it.

speaker.note: A coil in a magnetic field pushes a cone, and the cone pushes air.

spear.note: A point, a shaft, and the joint between them — which is the part that fails.

spine.note: The part that has to bend thousands of times and hold everything else.

spinneret.note: A plate of holes, and everything synthetic that is a fibre came out of one.

spirit_level.note: A bubble that is not there, and it goes to the top.

spline.note: Teeth along a shaft so it can slide and still turn what it is inside.

spoke.note: A wire in tension, which is why a bicycle wheel hangs rather than stands.

sputnik_1.note: A polished sphere with four aerials and a radio, and it changed everything.

stain.note: Making a colourless thing visible by binding a dye to part of it.

stained_glass.note: Colored glass held in lead cames, telling a story one piece at a time.

stand.note: Something that holds a thing at a height and does not fall over.

stand_mixer.note: Named for its beater's motion — spinning on its own axis while orbiting the bowl.

standard.note: An agreed thing to measure everything else against.

stator.note: The part that does not turn, and the part that makes the field.

stealth_aircraft.note: Faceted panels fling radar echoes away from the receiver.

steam_engine.note: In the order the steam travels: raise it, admit it, use it, condense it, and turn the push into a turn.

steam_locomotive.note: Steam pushes a piston; a connecting rod turns that push into a crank pin's rotation.

steering_wheel.note: The interface, and the last thing a crash tests.

structure.note: Anything that has to stand up under a load.

stryker_vehicle.note: Eight wheels trade off-road ability for road speed and quiet transit.

stupa.note: Solid all the way through. There is no interior, so the parts list is a mound and what is buried at the centre of it.

sukhothai.note: A Thai capital laid out around ponds cut to hold the wet season against the dry.

sundial.note: The earliest known sundials are Egyptian and Babylonian shadow clocks, dated to 1500 BCE.

surgical_scissors.note: Mayo for general cutting, Metzenbaum for delicate tissue.

survey.note: Fixing where things are, precisely enough to build from.

suspension.note: Keeping the wheels on the road while the body stays roughly still.

suture_needle.note: The thread is swaged in — no eye to load, unlike the older reusable kind.

suv.note: A tall body on a car platform, sold on the view.

sweater.note: Unscoured wool keeps its lanolin and sheds water.

symptom.note: What the patient reports, as opposed to what can be measured.

synagogue.note: Built around an ark that holds the Torah scrolls.

syndrome.note: A set of signs that keep turning up together before anyone knows why.

synthesizer.note: Generates its waveform electronically from scratch rather than amplifying a plucked string.

tabla.note: The black tuning spot — syahi — is iron-oxide paste; its mass tunes the drum.

tabulating_machine.note: Hollerith built it for the 1890 census; the company became IBM.

tailings_dam.note: Designed to hold its contents forever — often raised using the tailings themselves as fill.

tank_car.note: Some are lined in glass to hold acids; some wrap in a steam jacket to keep contents fluid.

tape.note: Drew's 1925 paper tape had a gentler adhesive for autobody painters.

tax.note: The state taking a share, and having to know enough about you to do it.

taxi.note: A car for hire, with a meter to stop the argument.

teapot.note: Called into being when China shifted from whipped to steeped tea.

telegraph.note: The first electric network, and it needed almost nothing: a key, a wire, and a code.

telephone.note: Sound to current and back again, with a way to say who you are calling.

temple.note: A house for a god, and usually not for a congregation.

tenaculum_forceps.note: A sharp hook, adapted from Civil War bullet forceps, grips tissue.

tesla_coil.note: Two coils tuned to the same resonant frequency step a spark-gap pulse up to millions of volts.

therapy.note: A structured attempt to change how somebody is doing.

theremin.note: The player's hand is a plate of a capacitor, so the instrument is deliberately incomplete until someone stands next to it.

tiger_tank.note: Flat, vertical armor — effective for its thickness, but heavy and expensive.

tikal.note: A Maya city of pyramids on a limestone shelf with no rivers at all.

tine.note: One prong of several, spaced so what you want passes and what you do not does not.

tire.note: Tread, sidewall, and bead hold air while steel belts hold the shape under load.

toilet.note: An S-shaped trap holds standing water that seals the drain against sewer gas.

tongs.note: Two levers on one pivot, so a hand can hold what a hand cannot.

toothbrush.note: William Addis carved the first mass-produced one from a bone handle in prison, 1780.

toron.note: The projecting sticks carry scaffolding for annual replastering and break up the mud surface.

tow_missile.note: Two hair-thin wires spool out behind it, carrying steering commands.

track_gauge.note: The distance between the rails, and the reason two railways cannot always meet.

trade.note: What has to exist before two strangers will exchange anything.

transformer.note: Two coils sharing one iron path, and the ratio between their turns is the whole device.

transistor.note: Two junctions in one crystal, so a small current can decide what a large one does.

treatment.note: What is actually done about a diagnosed condition.

tricycle.note: A third wheel trades a bicycle's need for balance for standing stability.

tripod.note: Three legs, because three points always define a plane and four wobble.

trocar.note: The sharp obturator punches through; the cannula stays.

truck.note: Body-on-frame: the cab is built separate from whatever it carries.

truss.note: Triangles only. Every member is in pure tension or pure compression, which is why it carries a span on a fraction of a beam's material.

tube.note: A hollow section, which is nearly as stiff as a solid one and a fraction of the weight.

tulwar.note: A curved saber of the Indian subcontinent, known by its all-metal disc pommel.

tumbler.note: The pin that blocks the plug until it is lifted exactly far enough.

tuner.note: Picking one frequency out of the air by making a circuit prefer it.

tuning_peg.note: Geared so a turn of the hand is a fraction of a turn at the string.

tunnel_boring_machine.note: A rotating cutterhead chews the tunnel face while hydraulic rams push the machine forward.

turbine.note: Blades on a shaft, and the only question is what is pushing them.

turboprop.note: A gas turbine that sends nearly all its power through a gearbox to the propeller.

tyre.note: The bead is a steel hoop that grips the rim; without it the tyre would blow off.

uhmwpe.note: Chains so long the material barely melts and almost nothing wears it.

umbilical_cord_clamp.note: Two jaws and a ratchet, sterile, single use.

universal_joint.note: Torque round a corner, at the cost of the speed varying twice a turn.

upholstery.note: Padding held under tension over a frame, so it keeps its shape when sat on.

vacuum_cleaner.note: A motor spins a fan, the fan drops pressure, and outside air rushes in through the nozzle.

vaginal_speculum.note: Cusco's duck-billed blades open like a hinge to reveal the cervix.

vault.note: It cannot stand until the last stone is in, so the whole thing is built on a temporary timber form and only becomes a vault when that comes away.

venturi.note: A narrowing where the flow speeds up and the pressure falls.

vexillum.note: Cloth hung from a crossbar, carried by Roman cavalry.

vhs.note: JVC's format beat Sony's sharper Betamax because its decks could record a feature in one pass.

vomitorium.note: The passage that lets a full amphitheatre empty in minutes.

voyager_program.note: Two probes on a planetary alignment that comes round every 176 years.

vulcanization.note: Sulfur bridges between rubber chains, so it stops being sticky and starts being elastic.

wall.note: Something to stand on, something to stack, and something to hold the stack together.

war_mace.note: Flanges concentrate force enough to dent plate — the answer to better armour.

warhead.note: The case, the filler, and the fuze that decides when. A warhead with no fuze is an inert lump, which is why the fuze is the part that is stored separately.

watch.note: A coiled mainspring replaced hanging weights, letting a clock's movement fit on a wrist.

weather_vane.note: An asymmetric pointer that swings to face into the wind — Athens' Tower of the Winds had one in 50 BC.

web_browser.note: A program that fetches a document and then argues with it.

webbing.note: Woven flat strap, stronger for its weight than the same fibre as rope.

wheel.note: A rim held off its centre by spokes, and something for it to turn on.

whistle.note: A pea rattling inside breaks the airstream into the characteristic trill.

whitfields_ointment.note: Benzoic acid to stop the fungus, salicylic acid to remove the skin it is in.

wii_remote.note: A camera tracks two IR LED clusters for pointing while an accelerometer reads tilt and shake.

winch.note: A drum, a gear reduction, and a brake — the brake being the part that matters.

window.note: A hole made weathertight without being made opaque.

wireless_telegraphy.note: Morse on spark-gap waves — across the Atlantic by 1901.

woad.note: Blue from a plant, by fermenting the leaves until the dye can be reduced.

wood_plastic_composite.note: Sawdust in a polymer, so it looks like timber and does not rot.

world_wide_web.note: Three inventions at once: an address, a protocol and a markup.

xor_gate.note: On when the inputs disagree, which is exactly what addition needs.

yataghan.note: A forward-curving blade with no guard, the hilt flared into two 'ears'.

yoyo.note: The string looped, not tied, around the axle is what lets it sleep.

zeppelin.note: A rigid, aluminum-framed airship whose shape is held by the frame, not by gas pressure.

zweihander.note: A sword scaled up past six feet, wielded two-handed by the Landsknechte's Doppelsöldner to break pike formations.

robot.note: An arm that moves through six axes, and the controller that plans where each joint should be at each instant.

starter_motor.note: The pinion engages only while cranking — a one-way clutch frees it the instant the engine catches.

windscreen.note: Laminated so it cracks but does not shatter — the plastic interlayer holds the fragments.

muffler.note: Sound waves bounce between chambers until they cancel themselves out.

hard_drive.note: The head floats on a cushion of air thinner than a fingerprint.

flap.note: Lowered to make a wing lift more at lower speeds — the price is drag.

touchscreen.note: The finger changes the capacitance, and a chip works out where.

anchor.note: The flukes dig in; the shank transmits the pull; the crown takes the beating.

lighthouse.note: The lens rotates so the flash has a signature — each lighthouse blinks its own pattern.

loudspeaker.note: A coil in a magnetic field glued to a cone — current in, sound out.

bushing.note: The insulator that lets high voltage pass through a grounded wall.

$not_assemblies_rule: A needs list answers 'what goes into one'. Some made things have no answer, and counting them as owing a list inflates the backlog until the sweep looks endless. A list is NOT owed for: a SHAPE or geometric feature (bevel, extrados, camber); a SURFACE or layer that is a coat of something already listed (scratch_coat, base_course); a JOINT or PROCESS (weld, tempering, honing); or a SINGLE PIECE of one material shaped by one operation (voussoir, quoin, link, shank). Each id here is a judgement somebody made and can be argued with — which is the point of writing it down rather than inferring it from tags, the way the first version of this denominator did.
$scope_rule: Which things OWE a parts list. The denominator was read off tags and counted 2,084, and about a third of that could never have had one: 321 were places, which already carry an `of` field naming what they are built of; 126 were dishes, where the recipe IS the parts list and a second one would just restate it; and 294 were drugs and diseases, which are not assembled at all. Excluding those leaves 1,343 artefacts that genuinely have a bill of materials. This is the fourth denominator in this project to have been wrong because it was inferred from tags rather than written down, after $not_assemblies, the coverage row for needs, and the places checklist figure — the pattern is consistent enough to expect.
